meta.title: Who really said "Not all readers are leaders, but all leaders are readers"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Truman wrote something close — but not this. His documented line: “Not all readers become leaders. But all leaders must be readers.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Not all readers are leaders, but all leaders are readers'?
meta.ogDescription: The popular phrasing is a later smoothing. Truman’s own words: “Not all readers become leaders. But all leaders must be readers.”

answer.label: Not Truman’s wording — a later paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Truman’s, but the sentence is not. What he actually put down was “Not all readers become leaders. But all leaders must be readers” — part of a longer note printed in Monte M. Poen’s edition of Truman’s unsent letters and desk notes ↗ and in Robert H. Ferrell’s edition of The Autobiography of Harry S. Truman ↗. The tidier “not all readers are leaders, but all leaders are readers” is a later smoothing that only turns up in books from the 1990s onward ↗, where it is credited to Truman, Zig Ziglar and John C. Maxwell more or less interchangeably.

source.excerpt: Readers of good books, particularly books of biography and history, are preparing themselves for leadership. Not all readers become leaders. But all leaders must be readers. Many readers become historians and teachers. They are retiring, timid when publicity is involved, and are among the …
trail: Search the scanned-book corpus for the popular sentence and nothing older than the 1990s comes back: every hit is a modern leadership or self-help title ↗, and they do not agree on who said it — Brian Tracy’s How the Best Leaders Lead credits Zig Ziglar, David Horsager’s The Trust Edge credits John C. Maxwell, others credit Truman.

Search instead for Truman’s own phrasing and it lands straight in his papers: “Not all readers become leaders. But all leaders must be readers” appears in both The Autobiography of Harry S. Truman and Strictly Personal and Confidential ↗.

The two editors disagree about where the words came from. Poen prints them under the heading “Desk Note [1950s]” ↗ — his other desk notes are dated handwritten memos from the President’s Secretary’s Files — while Ferrell’s edition attaches the editorial note “[President Truman speaking to a school group, 1960.]” ↗. We could not reconcile the two, so both are recorded here.

The catchy half of the modern version was already advertising copy before Truman wrote his note. Quote Investigator reproduces a 1917 advertisement in the Rockford Morning Star reading “ATTENTION SOLDIERS / LEADERS ARE READERS” ↗, and traces the cousin slogan “Today a reader, tomorrow a leader” to a student named W. Fusselman, printed in 1926.
source.excerptNote: Reconstructed from the full-text scans of both volumes. Poen’s transcription runs the first two sentences together with a colon and uses an ampersand (“historians & teachers”), the kind of shorthand typical of Truman’s handwriting; Ferrell’s prints full stops. Neither version contains the phrase people quote.

source.rightsNote: The earliest printing we could locate for Truman’s sentence is 1980, in Robert H. Ferrell’s The Autobiography of Harry S. Truman, with Monte M. Poen’s Strictly Personal and Confidential following in 1982 — both far too recent for the public domain, so the passage as published is in copyright. Being a president does not change that: these are personal notes and remarks issued by commercial and university presses, not federal work product. The reworded version in circulation has no identifiable author at all.

author.name: Harry S. Truman
author.heading: Harry S. Truman
author.bio: Truman was the last U.S. president who never earned a college degree, and he spent a lifetime compensating with books — a habit that began with the four-volume Great Men and Famous Women his mother gave him in 1894 and with a boyhood claim to have worked his way through the Independence public library. He genuinely believed that biography and history were leadership training, and said so often, which is why a sentence he never quite wrote sits so comfortably in his mouth. He took office in April 1945 on Franklin Roosevelt’s death, served until January 1953, and retired to Independence, Missouri, where he kept reading and writing.

cite.sourceCitation: Harry S. Truman, "Desk Note [1950s]," in Strictly Personal and Confidential: The Letters Harry Truman Never Mailed, ed. Monte M. Poen (Boston: Little, Brown, 1982). The same passage is printed in The Autobiography of Harry S. Truman, ed. Robert H. Ferrell (Boulder: Colorado Associated University Press, 1980), there carrying the editorial note "[President Truman speaking to a school group, 1960.]" Truman's wording is "Not all readers become leaders. But all leaders must be readers"; "Not all readers are leaders, but all leaders are readers" is a later paraphrase, located in print no earlier than the 1990s.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and who should
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabricated quote so much as a rewritten one. The sentiment is Truman’s; the sentence people share is not, and it has picked up several rival owners along the way.

items.why: Truman’s documented sentence reads “Not all readers become leaders. But all leaders must be readers,” as printed in both editions of his papers ↗. Even the Truman Library Institute’s own quotations page gives that form, with no source attached ↗.
Brian Tracy’s How the Best Leaders Lead introduces it as “Zig Ziglar said …” ↗, while another book on the same results page runs the identical sentence under Truman’s name.
David Horsager’s The Trust Edge attributes it to Maxwell in both of its editions ↗ — a fair sign the line had floated free of any named source.
“Leaders are readers” was a bookshop slogan long before it was a presidential quotation: Quote Investigator prints it in a 1917 Rockford Morning Star advertisement ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Truman’s real sentence — “Not all readers become leaders. But all leaders must be readers” — sits inside a longer passage about biography and history, printed in Strictly Personal and Confidential (Little, Brown, 1982) ↗ and in Ferrell’s edition of the autobiography. Quote it that way and you are quoting Truman.

context.heading: Why this one is so hard to shake
lead: Truman is a magnet for this kind of thing. He is remembered as the plain-spoken president — the desk sign, the short declarative sentence — so any tidy aphorism about self-improvement finds a home under his name. In this case the misattribution has an unusually good alibi: he really did write the thought down, in words that are almost, but not quite, the ones on the poster.

The give-away is the shape of the sentence. Truman’s version is two blunt sentences with a full stop between them — become and must be, verbs that do some work. The version in circulation is a single balanced epigram built on are and are, which reads beautifully and says slightly less. That is what happens to a line after a few decades of being retyped onto slides.
context.detailsSummary: The older slogan, and one loose end
detailsBody: The second half of the popular version was already in service before Truman put pen to paper: Quote Investigator reproduces a 1917 Rockford Morning Star advertisement selling military books under the banner “LEADERS ARE READERS”, and traces the related classroom slogan “Today a reader, tomorrow a leader” to a vocational-school student named W. Fusselman, printed in a Newark library journal in 1926.

There is one loose end we could not tie off. Poen’s 1982 volume presents the passage as a written desk note from the 1950s; Ferrell’s edition of the autobiography attaches an editorial note describing Truman speaking to a school group in 1960. Both are careful editors working from Truman’s papers, and we found no way to decide between them, so this page records both rather than picking the more quotable one.
context.pull: He wrote it as two sentences. The internet rewrote it as one.

sourcesVerified.claim: The Autobiography of Harry S. Truman and Strictly Personal and Confidential both contain the sentence "Not all readers become leaders. But all leaders must be readers."
Monte M. Poen's Strictly Personal and Confidential prints the passage beginning "Readers of good books" under the heading "Desk Note [1950s]".
The Autobiography of Harry S. Truman carries the editorial note "[President Truman speaking to a school group, 1960.]" adjacent to "leaders must be readers".
The wording "Not all readers are leaders, but all leaders are readers" appears only in modern books, credited to Truman among others, with no result shown dated before 1990.
Brian Tracy's How the Best Leaders Lead introduces the line as "Zig Ziglar said, 'Not all readers are leaders; but all leaders are readers.'"
David Horsager's The Trust Edge attributes "Not all readers are leaders, but all leaders are readers" to John C. Maxwell.

Quote Investigator reproduces a 1917 Rockford Morning Star advertisement reading "ATTENTION SOLDIERS / LEADERS ARE READERS" and concludes the slogan "Today a reader, tomorrow a leader" was probably created by a student named W. Fusselman, printed 1926; the article never mentions Truman.
The Truman Library Institute's quotations page prints "Not all readers become leaders. But all leaders must be readers." and gives no source for it.
Strictly Personal and Confidential: The Letters Harry Truman Never Mailed was edited by Monte M. Poen and published by Little, Brown, Boston, in 1982.

The Autobiography of Harry S. Truman is associated with editor Robert H. Ferrell and was originally published in Boulder, Colorado, by Colorado Associated University Press in 1980; this scan is the University of Missouri Press printing.
Wikiquote's Harry S. Truman page does not contain "Not all readers are leaders, but all leaders are readers" in any section.
